hs_math_t17_st01.title: Understanding Limits
hs_math_t17_st01.overview: A limit describes the value that a function approaches as its input approaches a specified number. It helps us study behaviour near a point, even when the function is not defined at that point.

key_concepts.definition: A limit concerns nearby input values, not necessarily the value at the target input.
details: When x approaches a, we examine values of x increasingly close to a from either side.
The outputs may approach a fixed number L even if f(a) is missing or has a different value.
A limit describes behaviour near a point rather than requiring the function to attain the limiting value.

key_concepts.definition: The notation states the input being approached and the output value approached.
details: In lim(x→a) f(x)=L, a is the target input and L is the limiting output.
Read it as: as x approaches a, f(x) approaches L.
The limit may exist even if f(a) is undefined.

key_concepts.definition: For polynomial functions and other functions continuous at the target, substitution gives the limit.
details: Replace x by the value it approaches and simplify.
For f(x)=x²+2x, as x approaches 3, the output approaches 15.
If substitution gives an undefined expression, that does not by itself determine the limit; other methods or further study may be needed.

key_concepts.definition: A function can be approached from smaller or larger input values.
details: The left-hand limit examines x-values less than a.
The right-hand limit examines x-values greater than a.
A two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.

visual_aids.title: A Function Approaching a Limit
visual_aids.caption: The output values approach L as the input approaches a from both sides.
visual_aids.alt_text: A curve approaches the same open point from the left and right, with dashed guides marking x=a and y=L.

worked_examples.problem: Evaluate $$\lim_{x\to 3}(x^2+2x)$$.
solution_steps: Substitute x=3 because the expression is a polynomial.

worked_examples.problem: A function has left-hand limit 4 and right-hand limit 4 at x=2, but f(2)=7. Find the limit.
solution_steps: Compare the two one-sided limits: both equal 4.
Since they agree, the two-sided limit exists and equals 4.
The separate function value 7 does not change the limit.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming the limit must equal f(a).
common_mistakes.correction: The limit describes nearby behaviour. The value f(a) may be different or undefined.

common_mistakes.mistake: Checking only one side of the target.
common_mistakes.correction: For a two-sided limit, compare the left-hand and right-hand behaviour.

quick_summary: A limit is the value approached by f(x) as x approaches a.
The value of the function at a can differ from the limit.
A two-sided limit exists only when the left- and right-hand limits agree.
Direct substitution is useful for polynomial functions.

hs_math_t17_st02.title: Limits from Graphs and Tables
hs_math_t17_st02.overview: Graphs and numerical tables provide visual and numerical ways to estimate limits. They help distinguish the value approached by a function from the value actually assigned at the target input.

key_concepts.definition: Trace the curve towards the target input from both directions.
details: Identify the target x-coordinate first.
Follow the graph from the left and right and estimate the y-value approached.
An open circle may show a missing function value while the curve still approaches that height.

key_concepts.definition: Choose input values increasingly close to the target from below and above.
details: For x approaching 2, values such as 1.9, 1.99 and 1.999 approach from the left.
Values such as 2.1, 2.01 and 2.001 approach from the right.
Compare the corresponding outputs and look for a common value.

key_concepts.definition: Different graph features lead to different conclusions about a limit.
details: At a hole, the curve may approach the same height from both sides, so the limit can exist.
At a jump, the left and right approaches are different, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
A graph's filled point gives f(a); the nearby curve indicates the limit.

key_concepts.definition: Tables and graphs provide estimates whose reliability depends on the scale and selected values.
details: Use values close to the target but avoid relying on rounded values alone.
Check both sides; one-sided data alone cannot establish a two-sided limit.
A graph may conceal small details, so use a table or algebraic reasoning when appropriate.

visual_aids.title: Graph and Table Evidence
visual_aids.caption: A hole can have a limit, while a jump gives different one-sided approaches.
visual_aids.alt_text: Two graph panels: a curve with a hole at the approached height and a jump with two distinct one-sided heights.

worked_examples.problem: Estimate the limit of (x²−4)/(x−2) as x approaches 2 using a table.
solution_steps: For x≠2, factor x²−4=(x−2)(x+2), so the expression equals x+2.
At x=1.9, the value is 3.9; at x=1.99, it is 3.99.
At x=2.01, the value is 4.01; at x=2.1, it is 4.1.

worked_examples.problem: A graph approaches y=3 from the left and y=5 from the right at x=1. Does the two-sided limit exist?
solution_steps: Because 3 and 5 are different, the two-sided limit does not exist.
worked_examples.final_answer: No; the one-sided limits are unequal.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the filled dot as the limit.
common_mistakes.correction: Trace the nearby curve towards the target. The filled dot indicates the function value, not necessarily the limit.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using values from only one side.
common_mistakes.correction: Compare values from both sides to assess a two-sided limit.

quick_summary: Use graphs by tracing the curve towards the target from both sides.
Use tables with input values close to the target on both sides.
A hole can have a limit; a jump with unequal one-sided values does not.
The filled point represents f(a), not automatically the limit.

hs_math_t17_st03.title: Continuity — Introduction
hs_math_t17_st03.overview: A function is continuous over a region when its graph has no break in that region. At this introductory level, continuity is recognised from graphs and simple functions; formal limit-based conditions are studied later.

key_concepts.definition: A continuous graph has no break, jump or missing point over the interval being considered.
details: The familiar pencil test is a useful visual guide: a continuous curve can be traced without lifting the pencil.
A hole or jump indicates a discontinuity.
Continuity is considered at a point or throughout an interval.

key_concepts.definition: A graph may fail to be continuous in several visible ways.
details: A removable break appears as a hole in an otherwise connected curve.
A jump occurs when the graph changes abruptly between different heights.
An infinite break occurs near a vertical asymptote, where values grow without bound in magnitude.

key_concepts.definition: Many elementary functions have continuous graphs throughout their natural domains.
details: Linear and polynomial functions are continuous for every real input.
A rational function is continuous wherever its denominator is not zero.
A square-root function is continuous on its real-valued domain.

key_concepts.definition: Continuity must be considered only where the function is defined.
details: For f(x)=1/(x−2), the function is not defined at x=2.
The graph has a vertical asymptote at x=2, so it is not continuous there.
A function may be continuous on separate intervals even if it is not continuous across a break.

visual_aids.title: Recognising Continuity
visual_aids.caption: A connected curve is continuous; holes and jumps show discontinuities.
visual_aids.alt_text: Three small graph panels showing a smooth connected curve, a hole and a jump.
visual_aids.data: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 220"><rect width="520" height="220" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc"/><g transform="translate(15 25)"><text x="70" y="10" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#0f172a">Continuous</text><path d="M10 120 Q70 10 130 120" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="4"/></g><g transform="translate(190 25)"><text x="70" y="10" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#0f172a">Hole</text><path d="M10 120 L70 45 M70 45 L130 120" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="4"/><circle cx="70" cy="45" r="6" fill="#fff" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/></g><g transform="translate(365 25)"><text x="70" y="10" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#0f172a">Jump</text><path d="M10 105 L70 105 M70 45 L130 45" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="4"/><circle cx="70" cy="105" r="5" fill="#fff" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="70" cy="45" r="5" fill="#dc2626"/></g></svg>

worked_examples.problem: State where f(x)=x²−1 is continuous.
solution_steps: Polynomial functions are continuous for all real values of x.

worked_examples.problem: Identify the discontinuity of f(x)=1/(x−3).
solution_steps: The denominator is zero when x−3=0, so x=3 is excluded from the domain.
The graph has a vertical asymptote at x=3.
The function is continuous on each side of x=3, but not at x=3.

worked_examples.problem: A graph is smooth except for an open circle at x=4. Name the type of break.
solution_steps: The curve approaches the missing point but the point itself is absent.
This is a hole, also called a removable discontinuity.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a graph is continuous wherever it looks smooth from far away.
common_mistakes.correction: Check for holes, jumps, excluded inputs and vertical asymptotes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignoring the domain.
common_mistakes.correction: A function cannot be continuous at an input where it is not defined.

quick_summary: Continuity means no break in the graph over the interval considered.
Holes, jumps and vertical asymptotes are common discontinuities.
Polynomials are continuous for all real inputs.
A rational function is continuous wherever its denominator is non-zero.

hs_math_t17_st04.title: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change
hs_math_t17_st04.overview: Rates of change describe how an output varies as an input changes. The average rate measures change over an interval; the instantaneous rate describes the rate at one input and is understood by considering intervals that become smaller.

key_concepts.definition: It compares the change in output with the change in input between two points.
details: For inputs x₁ and x₂, subtract the starting output from the ending output.
Divide by the corresponding change in input.
The result is the slope of the secant line joining the two points on the graph.

key_concepts.definition: A secant line intersects a curve at two points.
details: Its gradient gives the average rate of change over the interval.
A positive gradient means the ending output is greater than the starting output.
A negative gradient means the ending output is smaller; zero means the endpoint outputs are equal.

key_concepts.definition: It describes how rapidly the output is changing at one particular input.
details: Imagine choosing a second point very close to the point of interest.
As the interval becomes smaller, the secant gradient may approach a single value.
That limiting gradient is the instantaneous rate of change and is represented by the derivative when it exists.

key_concepts.definition: The rate of change has units of output per unit of input.
details: If distance is measured in kilometres and time in hours, the rate is kilometres per hour.
If cost is measured in currency and production in items, the rate is currency per item.
Always state whether a rate is average over an interval or instantaneous at a point.

visual_aids.title: Secant Slope Across an Interval
visual_aids.caption: The secant line joins two points; its gradient is the average rate of change.
visual_aids.alt_text: A curve with two marked points joined by a secant line and labelled horizontal and vertical changes.
visual_aids.data: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 220"><rect width="520" height="220" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="45" y1="180" x2="485" y2="180" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="70" y1="195" x2="70" y2="20" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M80 160 Q220 150 430 35" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="4"/><circle cx="150" cy="145" r="6" fill="#dc2626"/><circle cx="360" cy="75" r="6" fill="#dc2626"/><line x1="150" y1="145" x2="360" y2="75" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="150" y1="145" x2="360" y2="145" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="360" y1="145" x2="360" y2="75" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="2"/><text x="255" y="163" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#047857">change in x</text><text x="370" y="115" font-size="13" fill="#047857">change in y</text><text x="150" y="135" font-size="13" fill="#0f172a">A</text><text x="360" y="65" font-size="13" fill="#0f172a">B</text><text x="245" y="82" font-size="14" fill="#b91c1c">Secant line</text></svg>

worked_examples.problem: Find the average rate of change of f(x)=x²+2x from x=1 to x=3.
A car's position changes from 10 km to 70 km over 2 hours. Find its average velocity.
For f(x)=x², compare the average rate from x=2 to x=3 with the rate from x=2 to x=2.1.
solution_steps: The shorter interval gives a rate closer to the instantaneous rate at x=2, which is 4.
worked_examples.final_answer: 5 and 4.1; the rates approach 4 as the interval shrinks

common_mistakes.mistake: Reversing the subtraction in only one part of the formula.
common_mistakes.correction: Keep the output difference and input difference in the same order.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling an average rate the instantaneous rate.
common_mistakes.correction: An average rate applies to an interval; an instantaneous rate applies at one input.

common_mistakes.mistake: Omitting units in applied problems.
common_mistakes.correction: Use output units divided by input units.

quick_summary: Average rate of change is the slope of a secant line.
Instantaneous rate is approached as the interval shrinks.
Rates are measured in output units per input unit.
Distinguish interval rates from rates at a single point.

hs_math_t17_st05.title: Definition of a Derivative
hs_math_t17_st05.overview: The derivative gives the instantaneous rate of change of a function. It is defined through a limit of average rates of change and represents the gradient of the tangent to the curve when that gradient exists.

key_concepts.definition: The derivative at x=a is the limiting value of average rates as a nearby input approaches a.
details: Use the two inputs a and a+h, where h is a small non-zero change.
Calculate the change in function values and divide by h.
If the limit exists, it gives the instantaneous rate at a.

key_concepts.definition: Applying the limit definition with a variable input produces a new function.
details: The derivative function is written f′(x).
For each suitable input x, f′(x) gives the gradient of the original graph at that input.
The original function gives output values; the derivative gives rates of change.

key_concepts.definition: The derivative at a point is the gradient of the tangent line there.
details: A tangent line gives the local direction of the curve at the point.
The tangent gradient is the limit of secant gradients as the second point approaches the first.
At a sharp corner, the left and right tangent directions may disagree, so the derivative may not exist.

key_concepts.definition: Not every function has a derivative at every point.
details: A discontinuity prevents differentiability at that point.
A sharp corner such as y=|x| at x=0 has different one-sided slopes.
A vertical tangent may also prevent a finite derivative.

variables.a: Input at which the derivative is evaluated
variables.h: A non-zero input change approaching zero
variables.Condition: The derivative exists at the point under consideration
The derivative exists at the point under consideration

visual_aids.title: Secant Lines Approaching a Tangent
visual_aids.caption: As the second point approaches the first, the secant line approaches the tangent line.
visual_aids.alt_text: Curve with a fixed point, a nearby point, secant line and tangent line at the fixed point.

worked_examples.problem: Use the limit definition to find the derivative of f(x)=x² at x=3.
Explain why y=|x| has no derivative at x=0.
solution_steps: For x<0, the graph is a straight line with gradient −1.
For x>0, the graph is a straight line with gradient +1.
The one-sided gradients are different, so there is no single tangent gradient at x=0.
worked_examples.final_answer: The derivative does not exist at x=0

common_mistakes.mistake: Substituting h=0 before simplifying.
common_mistakes.correction: Keep h non-zero while simplifying the difference quotient; take the limit only after cancellation where valid.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing f(a) with f′(a).
common_mistakes.correction: f(a) is the function value; f′(a) is the instantaneous rate or tangent gradient.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming every point has a derivative.
common_mistakes.correction: Check for corners, discontinuities and other points where a unique finite tangent gradient does not exist.

quick_summary: The derivative measures instantaneous rate of change.
The derivative at a point is the tangent gradient.
The limit definition is built from average rates over shrinking intervals.
A derivative may fail to exist at corners or discontinuities.

hs_math_t17_st06.title: Basic Rules of Differentiation
hs_math_t17_st06.overview: Basic differentiation rules provide efficient ways to find derivatives of simple functions. At this level, the focus is on constants, powers, constant multiples, sums and differences.

key_concepts.definition: A constant function has no change in output, so its derivative is zero.
details: The graph of y=c is a horizontal line.
A horizontal line has gradient zero at every point.
Examples include the derivative of 7 and the derivative of π; both are zero.

key_concepts.definition: For a power of x, multiply by the exponent and reduce the exponent by one.
details: For xⁿ, bring n down as a coefficient.
Replace the exponent n by n−1.
This rule applies to the powers used in the lesson, including positive integer powers and simple negative or fractional powers where the function is defined.

key_concepts.definition: A constant factor remains as a multiplier when differentiating.
details: Differentiate the variable expression and keep the constant coefficient.
For example, the derivative of 5x³ is 5 times the derivative of x³.
This rule prevents the coefficient from being lost.

key_concepts.definition: Differentiate each term separately while preserving addition and subtraction.
details: Apply the relevant rule to each term.
Keep the original plus or minus signs between the differentiated terms.
A constant term contributes zero.

variables.n: Integer exponent; apply where x^n is defined and differentiable

visual_aids.title: Applying the Power Rule
visual_aids.caption: Bring the exponent down to multiply, then reduce the power by one.
visual_aids.alt_text: Example showing 4x⁵ differentiating to 20x⁴, with exponent 5 moved to coefficient and power reduced to 4.
visual_aids.data: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 220"><rect width="520" height="220" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="55" y="105" font-size="38" font-family="monospace" fill="#0f172a" font-weight="bold">4x⁵</text><path d="M145 70 Q190 25 230 75" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="230,75 218,69 220,82" fill="#dc2626"/><text x="160" y="35" font-size="14" fill="#b91c1c">5 × 4 = 20</text><text x="160" y="145" font-size="14" fill="#047857">5 − 1 = 4</text><path d="M265 105 L345 105" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="345,105 333,98 333,112" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="360" y="65" width="125" height="75" rx="8" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="422" y="110" text-anchor="middle" font-size="30" font-family="monospace" fill="#14532d" font-weight="bold">20x⁴</text></svg>

worked_examples.problem: Differentiate y=5x⁴−3x²+7x−9.
Differentiate f(x)=3/x².
solution_steps: Write with a positive exponent in the denominator.

worked_examples.problem: Differentiate g(x)=√x.
solution_steps: Rewrite using a square root in the denominator.

common_mistakes.mistake: Differentiating a constant as if it were a variable term.
common_mistakes.correction: A constant term differentiates to zero.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to reduce the exponent by one.
common_mistakes.correction: After multiplying by the exponent, subtract one from the original power.

common_mistakes.mistake: Losing a negative sign or coefficient.
common_mistakes.correction: Keep the coefficient and sign attached to each term throughout.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applying the power rule to a sum as though it were a product.
common_mistakes.correction: Differentiate each term separately using the sum or difference rule.

quick_summary: A constant differentiates to zero.
For xⁿ, multiply by n and reduce the power to n−1.
Keep constant coefficients when differentiating.
Differentiate sums and differences term by term.

hs_math_t17_st07.title: Derivatives of Polynomial Functions
hs_math_t17_st07.overview: A polynomial derivative is found by applying the basic differentiation rules to each term. The resulting derivative function can then be evaluated to find the gradient at a chosen input.

key_concepts.definition: Each polynomial term is differentiated separately.
details: Identify terms separated by plus or minus signs.
Apply the power rule to variable terms and the constant rule to the constant term.
Preserve the signs and combine the resulting terms.

key_concepts.definition: For a non-constant polynomial, differentiation reduces the highest power by one.
details: A cubic polynomial generally differentiates to a quadratic polynomial.
A quadratic polynomial generally differentiates to a linear polynomial.
A non-zero constant polynomial differentiates to zero.

key_concepts.definition: The derivative function gives the gradient at each input where it is defined.
details: First find the derivative function.
Then substitute the required x-value into the derivative.
Do not substitute into the original function when the question asks for the gradient.

key_concepts.definition: The sign and magnitude of the derivative describe the local slope.
details: A positive derivative indicates an upward slope.
A negative derivative indicates a downward slope.
A zero derivative indicates a horizontal tangent at that point.

visual_aids.title: Differentiate a Polynomial Term by Term
visual_aids.caption: Each term produces its own derivative; the constant term disappears.
visual_aids.data: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 220"><rect width="520" height="220" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="260" y="45" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" font-family="monospace" fill="#0f172a">4x³ − 5x² + 7</text><path d="M150 60 L150 95 M270 60 L270 95 M355 60 L355 95" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/><rect x="100" y="100" width="100" height="38" rx="6" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#2563eb"/><text x="150" y="125" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#1e3a8a">12x²</text><rect x="220" y="100" width="100" height="38" rx="6" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#2563eb"/><text x="270" y="125" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#1e3a8a">−10x</text><rect x="340" y="100" width="70" height="38" rx="6" fill="#f1f5f9" stroke="#94a3b8"/><text x="375" y="125" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#64748b">0</text><text x="260" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" font-family="monospace" fill="#047857">f′(x)=12x²−10x</text></svg>

worked_examples.problem: Differentiate f(x)=3x⁴−2x³+5x−6.
For f(x)=2x³−5x²+4x−8, find the gradient at x=2.
Find the point on y=x²−3x+2 where the tangent is horizontal.
solution_steps: A horizontal tangent has gradient zero, so 2x−3=0.
Substitute into the original function: y=9/4−9/2+2=−1/4.

common_mistakes.mistake: Substituting the point before differentiating.
common_mistakes.correction: Differentiate the original polynomial first, then evaluate the derivative at the given input.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping a term or changing its sign.
common_mistakes.correction: Work term by term and preserve each sign.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing the derivative value with the point's y-coordinate.
common_mistakes.correction: The derivative gives the gradient; use the original function to find the point's y-coordinate.

quick_summary: Differentiate every polynomial term separately.
The constant term becomes zero.
For a non-constant polynomial, the degree decreases by one.
Evaluate f′(a) to obtain the gradient at x=a.

hs_math_t17_st12.title: Tangents and Gradients of Curves
hs_math_t17_st12.overview: The derivative gives the gradient of a curve at a point. Once the point and gradient are known, the point-slope equation of a straight line can be used to form the tangent equation.

key_concepts.definition: The derivative evaluated at a point gives the tangent gradient.
details: Differentiate the function to obtain f′(x).
Substitute the x-coordinate of the point into f′(x).
The result is the gradient of the tangent at that point, provided the derivative exists.

key_concepts.definition: The point on the curve must satisfy the original function.
details: If only x=a is given, calculate y=f(a).
The tangent point is (a,f(a)).
Keep the original function for coordinates and the derivative for the gradient.

key_concepts.definition: Use the point-slope form of a straight line.
details: Substitute the tangent gradient for m.
Substitute the coordinates of the point for (x₁,y₁).
Simplify the resulting equation if required.

key_concepts.definition: The ordinary gradient formula describes finite slopes.
details: A horizontal tangent has gradient zero.
A vertical tangent has no finite gradient and cannot be written in the usual y=mx+c form.
At this level, focus on points where the derivative gives a finite tangent gradient.

visual_aids.caption: Differentiate for the slope, use the original function for the point, then apply point-slope form.

worked_examples.problem: Find the tangent to y=x² at x=2.
solution_steps: Find the point: y=2²=4, so the point is (2,4).
At x=2, the tangent gradient is m=4.

worked_examples.problem: Find the tangent to y=x³−x at x=1.
solution_steps: Point: y=1−1=0, so the point is (1,0).

worked_examples.problem: Find the gradient of y=2x²+3x at x=−1.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the derivative to find the y-coordinate.
common_mistakes.correction: Use the original function for the point and the derivative for the tangent gradient.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the wrong point in point-slope form.
common_mistakes.correction: Check that the point lies on the original curve before writing the tangent equation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming every tangent has a finite gradient.
common_mistakes.correction: A vertical tangent does not have a finite gradient in the usual slope formula.

quick_summary: The derivative at x=a gives the tangent gradient.
The original function gives the point (a,f(a)).
Use y−y₁=m(x−x₁) to form the tangent equation.
A horizontal tangent has gradient zero.

hs_math_t17_st13.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
hs_math_t17_st13.overview: The sign of the derivative indicates whether a differentiable function is increasing or decreasing over an interval. Simple sign tests help describe the behaviour of a graph.

key_concepts.definition: A function is increasing on an interval when its output rises as the input increases.
details: Where f′(x)>0 throughout an interval, the graph has a positive slope and is increasing there.
A positive derivative means the tangent slopes upward from left to right.
Use interval language to state where the function increases.

key_concepts.definition: A function is decreasing on an interval when its output falls as the input increases.
details: Where f′(x)<0 throughout an interval, the graph has a negative slope and is decreasing there.
A negative derivative means the tangent slopes downward from left to right.
Do not confuse a negative derivative with a negative function value.

key_concepts.definition: A stationary point can occur where the derivative is zero.
details: Solve f′(x)=0 to locate stationary inputs.
A stationary input divides the number line into intervals to test.
A zero derivative alone does not establish whether the point is a maximum or minimum.

key_concepts.definition: Testing the derivative in each interval identifies the direction of change.
details: Find the critical input values from f′(x)=0.
Choose a test value in each interval.
A positive result indicates increasing behaviour; a negative result indicates decreasing behaviour.

visual_aids.title: Derivative Sign and Direction
visual_aids.caption: Positive derivative indicates increasing behaviour; negative derivative indicates decreasing behaviour.
visual_aids.alt_text: A curve rises to a stationary point then falls, with positive and negative derivative regions marked.

worked_examples.problem: Find where f(x)=x²−4x+3 is increasing and decreasing.
solution_steps: For x<2, choose x=0: f′(0)=−4, so the function is decreasing.
For x>2, choose x=3: f′(3)=2, so the function is increasing.

worked_examples.problem: Determine the intervals of increase and decrease for f(x)=x³−3x.
solution_steps: Stationary inputs are x=−1 and x=1.
Test x=−2: f′(−2)=9>0, so increasing on (−∞,−1).
Test x=0: f′(0)=−3<0, so decreasing on (−1,1).
Test x=2: f′(2)=9>0, so increasing on (1,∞).

worked_examples.problem: What does f′(x)=0 tell us at a point?
solution_steps: The tangent gradient is zero at that input, so the tangent is horizontal.
The point is stationary, but further sign analysis is needed to classify it.
worked_examples.final_answer: It is a stationary point; it may be a maximum, minimum or another type of stationary point

common_mistakes.mistake: Testing intervals in the original function.
common_mistakes.correction: Use test values in the derivative, because its sign gives the direction of change.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming f′(x)=0 always means a maximum or minimum.
common_mistakes.correction: Check whether the derivative changes sign across the stationary input.

common_mistakes.mistake: Including a stationary endpoint in an open interval without explanation.
common_mistakes.correction: State intervals carefully and handle domain endpoints separately where relevant.

quick_summary: Positive derivative means increasing; negative derivative means decreasing.
Solve f′(x)=0 to locate stationary inputs.
Use a sign chart to test each interval.
A stationary point is not automatically a maximum or minimum.

hs_math_t17_st14.title: Stationary Points — Introduction
hs_math_t17_st14.overview: A stationary point is a point on a differentiable curve where the tangent is horizontal. Introductory graphical reasoning can identify simple local maxima and minima by observing whether the curve changes direction.

key_concepts.definition: A stationary point occurs where the derivative is zero.
details: At a stationary point, the tangent is horizontal.
Solve f′(x)=0 to find candidate x-coordinates.
Substitute each candidate into the original function to find its y-coordinate.

key_concepts.definition: A local maximum is a point higher than nearby points on the graph.
details: The graph rises before the point and falls after it.
In a derivative sign chart, the derivative changes from positive to negative.
The point is a local peak, not necessarily the highest value over the entire domain.

key_concepts.definition: A local minimum is a point lower than nearby points on the graph.
details: The graph falls before the point and rises after it.
In a derivative sign chart, the derivative changes from negative to positive.
The point is a local valley, not necessarily the lowest value over the entire domain.

key_concepts.concept: Not every stationary point is an extremum
key_concepts.definition: A horizontal tangent does not guarantee a peak or valley.
details: A curve may flatten and continue increasing or decreasing.
For example, y=x³ has a horizontal tangent at x=0 but continues increasing on both sides.
Use the graph or sign change to decide whether the stationary point is a local maximum or minimum.

visual_aids.title: Local Maximum and Minimum
visual_aids.caption: A local maximum changes from increasing to decreasing; a local minimum changes from decreasing to increasing.
visual_aids.alt_text: Two curve sketches: hill and valley with horizontal tangents and direction arrows.

worked_examples.problem: Find and classify the stationary point of f(x)=x²−6x+5.
solution_steps: The parabola opens upwards, so this stationary point is a local minimum.

worked_examples.problem: Find the stationary point of f(x)=−x²+4x+1 and classify it.
solution_steps: The parabola opens downwards, so the stationary point is a local maximum.

worked_examples.problem: Is the stationary point of y=x³ at x=0 a local maximum or minimum?
solution_steps: Differentiate: y′=3x², which is zero at x=0.
For x<0 and x>0, the derivative is positive except at zero.
The function increases on both sides, so it does not change direction.
worked_examples.final_answer: Neither; it is a stationary point but not a local maximum or minimum

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling every stationary point an extremum.
common_mistakes.correction: Check the graph or the derivative sign on both sides.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reporting only the x-coordinate.
common_mistakes.correction: Substitute the stationary input into the original function to obtain the full point.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing local and absolute extrema.
common_mistakes.correction: A local extremum is compared with nearby values; an absolute extremum is compared with the entire domain.

quick_summary: A stationary point has a horizontal tangent and f′(a)=0.
A + to − sign change indicates a local maximum.
A − to + sign change indicates a local minimum.
A stationary point need not be a maximum or minimum.

hs_math_t17_st16.title: Simple Indefinite Integrals
hs_math_t17_st16.overview: Integration reverses differentiation. An indefinite integral represents a family of functions whose derivatives equal the given function. At this level, integrate simple polynomial terms and verify answers by differentiating.

key_concepts.definition: An antiderivative of a function is a function whose derivative is the original function.
details: If F′(x)=f(x), then F is an antiderivative of f.
A function can have many antiderivatives that differ by a constant.
Differentiating an antiderivative returns the original integrand.

key_concepts.definition: The integral sign represents the family of antiderivatives.
details: In ∫f(x) dx, f(x) is the integrand and x is the variable of integration.
The symbol dx indicates integration with respect to x.
The constant of integration +C must be included because the derivative of any constant is zero.

key_concepts.definition: For a power xⁿ with n not equal to −1, increase the power by one and divide by the new power.
details: Add 1 to the exponent.
Divide the coefficient by the new exponent.
The rule applies term by term to simple polynomial expressions.

key_concepts.definition: Integrate each term separately while retaining coefficients and signs.
details: The integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals.
A constant multiplier can be taken outside the integral.
Integrate constant terms as constant multiples of x.

key_concepts.definition: Differentiate the proposed antiderivative to verify it.
details: Differentiate the answer term by term.
The result should equal the original integrand.
The constant C disappears when differentiated.

visual_aids.title: Integration as Reverse Differentiation
visual_aids.caption: Integration reverses differentiation: x³ differentiates to 3x², so 3x² integrates to x³+C.
visual_aids.alt_text: Arrow from x³ to 3x² labelled differentiate and reverse arrow labelled integrate.

worked_examples.problem: Evaluate ∫6x² dx.
solution_steps: Divide the coefficient 6 by 3 to obtain 2.

worked_examples.problem: Evaluate ∫(4x³−6x+5) dx.
Find an antiderivative of 8x³+2x and verify it.
Evaluate ∫7 dx.
solution_steps: The integral of a constant k is kx+C.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the constant of integration.
common_mistakes.correction: Always include +C in an indefinite integral.

common_mistakes.mistake: Subtracting one from the power as in differentiation.
common_mistakes.correction: Integration increases the exponent by one, then divides by the new exponent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing by the old exponent.
common_mistakes.correction: Divide by n+1 after increasing the power from n to n+1.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not checking the result.
common_mistakes.correction: Differentiate the proposed antiderivative and confirm that it returns the integrand.

quick_summary: Integration is the reverse process of differentiation.
Increase the power by one and divide by the new power.
Integrate polynomial sums term by term.
Include +C in every indefinite integral.
Differentiate your answer to verify it.
